Land Transport and Related Matters Bill, Second Reading debate

Second Reading3 February 2026 – 4 February 2026 bill-780, bill-781

A Second Reading debate on the Land Transport and Related Matters Bill, an omnibus Bill by the Ministry of Transport and Ministry of Home Affairs that amends road traffic, active mobility, ERP 2.0, speed limiter and related laws.

The Bill decriminalises missed ERP charges and makes the On-Board Unit mandatory for all Singapore-registered vehicles from 1 January 2027. It lowers the speed limit for mobility vehicles on public paths to six kilometres an hour from 1 June 2026, requires a Certificate of Medical Need for mobility scooter users on public paths, and introduces registration and penalties. It also raises penalties for illegal vehicle modifications and unregistered or deregistered vehicles, and updates speed limiter offences.

Parliament approves grants to IMF trust funds for low-income countries and Sudan's debt relief

4 February 2026 motion-2838

Two Motions moved by Minister of State Alvin Tan under section 6A(2)(d) of the Bretton Woods Agreements Act 1966, asking Parliament to fix the maximum amount of grants the Monetary Authority of Singapore may give to the IMF's Poverty Reduction and Growth Trust and to the PRG-HIPC Trust for Sudan's debt relief, debated together and voted on separately.

The transcript states that the grant to the Poverty Reduction and Growth Trust will draw from Singapore's 2021 SDR allocation and reduce MAS' official foreign reserves by 21 million SDR, about US$28.6 million, while the grant to the PRG-HIPC Trust will be funded from Singapore's share of the IMF's existing resources and will not affect the size of MAS' official foreign reserves. Minister of State Alvin Tan said the contributions do not draw on past reserves and will not affect or reduce domestic expenditure for Singaporeans. The money supports the IMF's concessional lending to low-income countries and Sudan's debt relief under the Heavily Indebted Poor Countries Initiative.

      Verbatim43 words

Parliament approves maximum grant for Sudan debt relief via IMF trust

4 February 2026 motion-2839

A motion under section 6A(2)(d) of the Bretton Woods Agreements Act 1966, moved by Minister of State for Trade and Industry Alvin Tan on behalf of the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister-in-charge of the Monetary Authority of Singapore, setting the maximum amount MAS may give under a bilateral agreement with the International Monetary Fund to support Sudan's debt relief efforts.

The resolution caps the grant that the Monetary Authority of Singapore may give under a bilateral agreement with the International Monetary Fund at 4,480,000 Special Drawing Rights (approximately US$6,100,000). The money is to support Sudan's debt relief efforts via the Trust for Special Poverty Reduction and Growth Operations for the Heavily Indebted Poor Countries. The record does not set out further practical impact for people in Singapore.

  • Mr Alvin Tan

    • Alvin Tan moved that Parliament resolve the maximum grant MAS may give under a bilateral agreement with the IMF to support Sudan's debt relief efforts is 4,480,000 Special Drawing Rights (approximately US$6,100,000).

      Verbatim7 words

  • Mr Speaker

    • The motion was resolved as moved.

      Verbatim35 words
      Resolved, "That this Parliament, in accordance with section 6A(2)(d) of the Bretton Woods Agreements Act 1966, resolves that the maximum amount of grants that the Monetary Authority of Singapore may give under the bilateral agreement

    • No other Members spoke again.

      Verbatim10 words
      are there any other Members wish to speak again? No?
Open questions from this debate (4)

Questions the debate raises that the record does not resolve. Listed as open questions, not as findings.

  • What are the terms of the bilateral agreement between MAS and the IMF?
  • How will the Trust for Special Poverty Reduction and Growth Operations for the Heavily Indebted Poor Countries use the funds?
  • What is the total amount of Sudan's debt relief effort?

An Adjournment Motion in which Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng raised resident disamenities from commercial activity in residential neighbourhoods and proposed six measures, followed by a response from Senior Minister of State Sun Xueling.

Residents in mixed-use neighbourhoods may be affected by noise, smell, safety and congestion from nearby commercial activity, and the debate sets out existing and proposed measures such as HDB tenancy conditions, quotas on licensed massage establishments, exclusion areas for new nightlife or massage outlets, and a review of massage establishment regulations. The transcript does not state a commencement date or final decision on the six proposals.

What happens next SPF is currently reviewing the massage establishment regulations; industry consultation will be done in due course. Members are encouraged to submit COS cuts using the online system. Parliament adjourned accordingly at 6.49 pm.

Open questions from this debate (8)

Questions the debate raises that the record does not resolve. Listed as open questions, not as findings.

  • Which, if any, of the six proposals will the Government adopt?

  • When will the industry consultation on massage establishment regulations take place?
  • How would good neighbour agreements be implemented or enforced?
  • What criteria are used to designate exclusion areas for new nightlife or massage establishments?
  • How will agencies measure or address local concentration of commercial activities?
  • Will the Massage Establishments Exemption Order 2018 be amended?
